cim: Students and artificial intelligence industry leaders connect at inaugural Michigan AI Business Conference
cim_eredeti: Students and artificial intelligence industry leaders connect at inaugural Michigan AI Business Conference
szoveg_eredeti:
More than 250 students, professors and industry leaders gathered Friday for the first Michigan Artificial Intelligence Business Conference at the Ross School of Business. The conference featured panelists and speakers from Citi, Bank of America, J.P. Morgan and Microsoft. The event was organized by AI Business Group and affiliated with the Business School, School of Engineering and School of Information.

The conference aimed to connect students with professionals, who spoke about how artificial intelligence is impacting the business world.

Business sophomore Michael Koury, vice president of conferences for ABG, wrote in an email to The Michigan Daily that the group’s goal was to provide both insight and connections for students.

“Our goal was to put students in the room with people who are actually using AI at work, not just reading about it,” Koury wrote. “A lot of us are recruiting into careers that AI is already changing, so we wanted the day to be practical, with real conversations with speakers, a chance to meet recruiters, and something students could use right away.”

Jennifer Marsman, keynote speaker and principal engineer in AI at Microsoft, told attendees how businesses are leveraging AI in their operations. She said Microsoft has recently utilized AI to increase productivity through their Microsoft Copilot Checkout partnership with Etsy to turn user searches into specialized product recommendations.

Marsman said other utilizations of AI across industries include journalists using AI models to speed up the editing process, retailers implementing models for personalized clothing recommendations and fast food chains operating drive-thrus with speech-to-text models.

While Marsman spoke highly of AI’s capabilities, she also recognized industries must be cautious about leaning on AI too much. She recommended creating a balance of AI use and human-based roles to ensure learning is still incentivized as the industry evolves.

“As it’s getting easier and easier to have something do your thinking for you, make sure you are still exercising your mind,” Marsman said. “It’s so important. People who stay curious, who want to learn, who want to understand what’s happening underneath — those are the people who are going to be successful.”

Marsman also explained the work AI can do beyond business, highlighting her work on a team at Microsoft specifically focused on environmental efforts called AI for Earth. The team focused on infectious disease spread research by analyzing mosquitoes using AI-powered traps that would identify and capture mosquitoes based on their wingbeat patterns. They also developed an anti-poaching project using drones with infrared cameras monitored by AI to track animals and identify poachers.

In an interview with The Daily, Business sophomore Lia Toltzman said hearing about AI for Earth provided an interesting new perspective on AI, and how its usage extends beyond what she originally thought.

“Hearing from Jennifer’s experiences in such a diverse mix of AI usages, such as AI for Earth, was really cool,” Toltzman said. “AI being used for environmental purposes was something that I hadn’t really considered before because I feel like everyone associates AI with tech for the most part.”

In addition to learning more about AI, some attendees described how their career goals shifted after hearing from professionals at the conference. LSA sophomore Chanse Rivera said the conference redirected his interest toward the technical aspect of business.

“After this conference, I’m more interested in doing the technical side of things as opposed to just a client-based thing,” Rivera said. “I feel like a lot of people are talking about how being in front of clients is very important in the AI age because it’s the last thing that can’t be automated, but I still think there’s a lot of room for technical growth and technical opportunities.”

Daily Staff Reporter Hannah Hiller and Alexandra Sim can be reached at hkhiller@umich.edu and alexfsim@umich.edu.
